Opinion: Grand Theft Auto VI and World of Warcraft: Forever show that mundanity is having a moment
Two of the year's biggest hits tell us that downtime and doldrums can be as compelling as dungeons and dragons.
Bryant Francis
,
Senior Editor
,
GameDeveloper.com
November 24, 2026
schedule
7 Min Read
expand_content
Image via Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive
It's been 20 years since I last played Blizzard Entertainment's
World of Warcraft
. But when my friend group cajoled me into picking up
World of Warcraft: Forever
,
I finally broke down and embraced the nostalgia of returning to the Azeroth of my youth. I rolled a Retribution Paladin, just as I did before. I raced to cut down Kobolds and Defias Bandits, feeling old instincts come alive. I was ready to set out on my grand adventure and see every fantastic quest, and every interesting new quality-of-life update that's been added to Blizzard's unprecedented revival experiment.
Then two hours later, I was in the Deeprun Tram. Waiting for a train. For the full 72 seconds. It felt like ten minutes. And I thought to myself "wait, is this supposed to be fun?"
But of course it is. Just like sitting by the campfire for a minute to get skill bonuses is fun. Just like waiting for my friends to arrive at a dungeon is fun. And just like running through a city with no speed buffs is fun. I'd forgotten that in 2004, before the UX of so many games became about supercharging dopamine hits as fast as possible, building worlds so large that waiting was on some level, necessary, was an awe-inspiring feat.
Related:
Is Control Resonant's protagonist a 'sad wet man?' ft. Mikael Kasurinen
It's tempting to write this off as nostalgia for a simpler time. But a funny thing happened: Rockstar Games'
Grand Theft Auto VI
came out. And before the game was even out, I was learning how players were people meticulously painting the walls of a house, building IKEA furniture, and putting coffee cups in the sink.
"That's weird," I thought. "All I saw in
Grand Theft Auto V
was shooting and driving." But in the years since my out-of-work roommate and I lazed about playing
GTA V
, Rockstar Games had experimented with wild simulation technology in
Red Dead Redemption 2
. Now here it is in full display, bringing the little tasks of modern life to big-budget gameplay.
Two examples doesn't make for a trend, but two high-profile, massively successful examples is worth calling my shot: both of these games are telling us something important: players don't just need to be cajoled through bright likes, juicy animation, and over-signaled level design. They want to relax with life's simple pleasures—they just don't want doing so to feel as frustrating as it can in the real world.
What makes these games' chores so interesting?
Metaverse boosters from 2021-2022 may be frothing at the mouth at this trend. They worked so hard to bring the real world to the digital one, and players roundly rejected them. "Why won't people live in our digital worlds?" they ask.
Related:
Clair Obscur: Expedition 33's narrative lead wants to change game funding
The best answer comes from
YouTube essayist Dan Olson
, who broke down how so much Metaverse design theory recreated the friction of the real world that our brains are usually good at scrubbing out. But games are played either on 2D monitors or 3D VR headsets, and recreating this friction has narrow appeal, especially when it risks making players ask "why am I spending my free time doing things I have to do in real life?"
The key word there is "have to do."
WoW: Forever
and
GTA VI
carefully limit the mandatories of their mundane moments, and have each clearly tested how much friction their players are willing to tolerate. Observe in
GTA VI
how the wall-painting minigame doesn't require you to deal with the annoyance of laying out paint tarp. Its furniture-building experience doesn't force you to combine physical dexterity and hand-eye coordination with complex instructions.
Image via Blizzard Entertainment/Xbox
The chores of
WoW: Forever
also spotlight how pleasant UX experiences can substitute real-life frustration and make the act of standing still and waiting for time to pass a purer moment. On the one hand, I'm annoyed when I need 60 seconds to turn 100 linen cloth into bandages. On the other hand, the little "wuh-wuhmp" noise that accompanies each act is music to my ears. Same goes for the sizzling of smelting minerals. And the "clank" of blacksmithing weapons and armor.
Related:
What Rami Ismail learned during his return to game development
But hark—I hear another class of game developers banging on my window. "We've been doing this for ages!" they shout. "We know players love this!" Fear not my friends, because indeed, we must talk about how this groundwork was laid by the hundreds of developers in the simulation genre.
The simulation genre has long served this need
In the last few years you've probably read many articles about the phenomenon of players enjoying "games as work," that describe how these games serve needs not being met by our real-life jobs under capitalism. I'll let critics like
Cameron Kunzleman
,
Steph Coelho
, and
Michael Piantini
tell you more about that. I'm certainly familiar with this dynamic—one of my favorite games in 2025 was
News Tower
, where I acted as editor-in-chief for a premiere paper in New York City. As if I didn't have enough angry people criticizing my writing at my day job.
But simulation design isn't just about identifying what players want to do, it's dialing in how they do it. And these studios have cooked up such a spectrum of design ideas. We have game store simulators to scratch the itch of opening packs. We have fishing games for real-life fisherman to play in the off-season. We have the entire European constellation of vehicle simulation games, which I can't even begin to wrap my head around because
